source_read: PDF (version of record), Lancet 2024;403:1779-1788, all 10 pages; text extracted with pdftotext -layout; every number used checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, with Table 1, Figure 1, Table 2 and Figure 2 also at 300 dpi. The online appendix and the published protocol were not among the files and were not read.

claims.overstatement: Mild, in three places. (1) The reason the first week starts on day 2 is stated as fact ('deaths in custody had been recorded as deaths on the day of release, which inflated the release-day rate'); the paper hedges throughout: data 'suggested' some cohorts 'might have' miscoded (p. 1781), the day-1 spike is 'probably at least partially an artefact' (p. 1784) and such deaths 'may have been' miscoded (p. 1786). Suggest 'may have been recorded ... probably inflating'. (2) The days 2-7, week-by-week and more-than-1-year rates, the IRRs and the release-day rate are attributed to the 18 cohorts in eight countries; Figure 2's caption (p. 1785) says the time-period analyses excluded the two cohorts that could not give deaths by day (Cunningham and King, New Zealand's only cohort, and Binswanger, Washington State), so these rest on 16 cohorts in seven countries. The 725, 146, 16,126, 75,427 and 236-1,183 figures do use all 18. (3) 'Causes ... were not checked across countries and decades' is better worded as 'the paper reports no check of certification or coding': the paper is silent rather than stating that no check was made. Minor: 'everyone released' is the paper's own description, but one cohort (Rosen, North Carolina 1980-1999) contained only men (Table 1; Table 2 footnote).
claims.note: Every number from this source in the statement and magnitude was found on the rendered pages and matches: 1,471,526; 88.3% (1,299,322 male); 75,427; 1612 (1048-2287), I2 91.1%; 725 (625-831); 737 (636-844); IRRs 1.5 (1.2-1.8), 2.0 (1.5-2.6), 2.2 (1.6-3.0); 4036 (887-8940) and 826 (0-3455) in ten cohorts; 657 (332-1076), 135 (36-277), 71 (16-153); 146 (103-197); 16,126 (21.4%); 14,671 (91.0%); 236 and 1183; Europe 2762 (1832-3872), USA 934 (389-1703); 720 (605-845) in 16 cohorts. Recomputed: 16,126/75,427 = 21.4%; 14,671/16,126 = 91.0% (so 1,455 such deaths within 4 weeks); 1,299,322/1,471,526 = 88.3%; per-cohort deaths/person-years in Table 1 reproduce every Figure 1 rate (Lim 236, Fazel and Chang 1183). The paper does not say whether 'more than 4 weeks after release' counts from the index release or from the most recent release, or whether the release day is included. A rough check (my inference, approximate because pooled rates are not crude totals): the pooled poisoning rates for days 2-7, week 2 and weeks 3-4 imply about 420 such deaths in the first 4 weeks after the index release across 1.47 million people, far fewer than 1,455, so the count probably uses time since each release. The editors' explanation (most person-time lies beyond the first weeks) is consistent with the paper: median follow-up 3.1 to 18.1 years per cohort (Table 1) and 10.5 million person-years. The study's own analyses compare post-release periods only (IRRs between periods, p. 1781); comparisons with the general population appear only as background from earlier studies (pp. 1779-1780). Risk factors examined were limited to age and sex, and there was no information on what happened between release and death (p. 1786); the paper never mentions tolerance. The 'alcohol and other drug poisoning' category is one Table 2 row (unintentional and undetermined intent, underlying cause by ICD-9/10, codes in appendix p 8, not seen); the Discussion calls the same deaths 'overdose deaths'. Reporting points found: overall all-cause I2 is 100% in the text and Figure 1 but 98.8% in Table 2; Table 1 prints Liu's female share as 1.6% (7215/62,425 = 11.6%); Table 1 female and male column totals (172,204; 1,299,322) differ by 360 each from the sums of the rows (172,564; 1,298,962), and total person-years by 225 (10,534,441 printed, 10,534,666 summed); the Methods sentence that all post-release time was counted 'minus any time spent reincarcerated' (p. 1781) is ambiguous, since the sensitivity analysis that excludes time and deaths while reincarcerated (720) is presented as a departure from the primary analysis (p. 1783); it most likely applies only to the any-release analyses.

anchors.extracted: Linked administrative data on 1,471,526 people released from prison or jail in eight countries (Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden, USA), 1980-2018, 10,534,441 person-years; 18 cohorts pooled by two-step IPD meta-analysis into crude mortality rates (CMR) per 100,000 person-years for set periods after release. 75,427 deaths. First-week all-cause CMR 1612 (95% CI 1048-2287), higher than every other period: IRR vs week 2 1.5 (1.2-1.8), I2 26.0%; vs weeks 3-4 2.0 (1.5-2.6), I2 53.0%; vs weeks 9-12 2.2 (1.6-3.0), I2 70.5%. Highest first-week cause-specific CMRs: alcohol and other drug (AOD) poisoning 657 (332-1076), suicide 135 (36-277), cardiovascular disease 71 (16-153).

anchors.locator: Methods, Study design and data sources, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Consortium cohorts link incarceration records with national or state death registers. The 18 cohorts analysed are unselected: everyone released during each study period, not cohorts built on a health condition or a type of offence; they are 98% of the consortium (n = 1,471,526) and come from the eight named countries. (The 88%/12% split with n = 1,321,812 / 180,195 in the 2nd paragraph refers to the whole 30-cohort consortium of 1,502,007.)

anchors.locator: Methods, Data analysis, 2nd-4th paragraphs and 8th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Follow-up runs from release from the first incarceration in the study period (index); periods: days 1-14 daily, weeks 3-12 weekly, weeks 13-52, week 53 onwards, total; aggregation of later weeks decided post hoc. Causes coded from ICD-9/10 underlying cause of death into a two-level, mutually exclusive scheme (appendix p 8). Random-effects pooled CMRs with Freeman-Tukey transformation; pooled IRRs compare post-release periods with one another (no general-population comparison). Sex from correctional records; covariates limited to age and sex.

Day-1 data suggested that in some cohorts people who died in custody might have been coded as released and dying on the release day; ten cohorts could definitively separate custody deaths from post-release deaths; for this reason the primary analyses start observation on the first full 24-hour day after release (labelled day 2) in all cohorts.

All cohorts from high-income countries (North America, Europe, Australasia) except one Brazilian cohort. 1,471,526 people: 1,299,322 (88.3%) male, 172,204 (11.7%) female; 10,534,441 person-years; 75,427 deaths. All-cause pooled CMR after index release 725 (95% CI 625-831), I2 = 100%.

Leading causes over the whole follow-up: AOD poisoning CMR 146 (103-197), I2 99.7%; cardiovascular disease 102 (85-119); cancer 74 (61-88). AOD poisoning 21.4% of deaths; injuries 37,425 (49.7%). No significant age difference in AOD poisoning rates. Table 1: cohort sizes 6,375 to 258,617; median follow-up 3.1 to 18.1 years (range 0-24); Rosen cohort (North Carolina, 1980-1999) all male.

All-cause CMR highest in days 2-7 after index release, 1612 (1048-2287), I2 91.1%, falling to 737 (636-844), I2 99.6%, more than 1 year after release (Figure 2; appendix p 26). First week significantly higher than all other periods; IRRs 1.5 (1.2-1.8), 2.0 (1.5-2.6), 2.2 (1.6-3.0) vs week 2, weeks 3-4 and weeks 9-12. Days 2-7 cause-specific: AOD poisoning 657 (332-1076), I2 89.0%; suicide 135 (36-277), I2 71.0%; cardiovascular 71 (16-153), I2 45.7%. AOD poisoning above every other cause across the first 2 weeks, highest point estimate in all periods, and the only cause whose rate peaked in the first week.

Days 2-7 all-cause CMR highest in Europe 2762 (1832-3872), I2 70.7%, lowest in the USA 934 (389-1703), I2 92.0% (appendix p 28); regional differences attenuated over time, none detectable after more than 1 year.

16 of 18 cohorts recorded reincarceration (1,309,958 people, 89.0%; 8,324,428 person-years; 56,731 deaths). Excluding time and deaths while reincarcerated, all-cause CMR 720 (605-845), almost the same as 725 (625-831).

In the ten cohorts that could say definitively whether a death occurred in custody or after release, the release-day CMR fell from 4036 (887-8940; I2 96.9%) to 826 (0-3455; I2 95.2%) (appendix p 25); rates in other periods were similar to the main analysis; overall all-cause CMR in these ten cohorts 693 (557-845).

Whole-follow-up all-cause CMR by cohort ranged from 236 (225-248; Lim, USA, New York) to 1183 (1141-1227; Fazel and Chang, Sweden); overall 725 (625-831), I2 100%; between-region heterogeneity p = 0.017.

Alcohol and other drug poisoning (unintentional and undetermined intent): 16,126 deaths, CMR 146 (103-197), I2 99.7%, a single category with no breakdown by substance; all-cause 75,427 deaths, 725 (625-831) (I2 printed 98.8% here vs 100% in the text). Suicide 6,199 deaths, 67 (49-87).

Of the 16,126 deaths the Discussion calls overdose deaths, 14,671 (91.0%) occurred more than 4 weeks after release; the authors conclude that acute post-release prevention alone would reach only a small minority of them. Which release the 4 weeks are counted from (index or most recent) is not stated.

anchors.locator: Figure 2, panels A and B and caption
anchors.extracted: Daily all-cause CMRs for days 2-14 and pooled rates for later periods; cause-specific panel shows AOD poisoning highest in every period, from about 657 in days 2-7 down to about 150 in weeks 53 and over. Caption: the Cunningham and King (New Zealand) and Binswanger (Washington) cohorts could not provide deaths by day and were excluded from these time-period analyses, so the period-specific rates rest on 16 cohorts.

No records of incarcerations before the index one; nearly all cohorts from high-income countries; individual risk factors limited to age and sex; no information on what happened between release and death; eight of 18 cohorts could not separate custody deaths from release-day deaths, which may have been miscoded, inflating day-1 estimates.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 matches the card's design (meta-analysis), and critically low follows from items 9, 13 and 15, as the card says. Items 4, 7 and 15 fit an IPD consortium of population registries poorly; the substantive weakness is items 9 and 13: no appraisal of linkage or of cause-of-death certification and coding across eight countries and four decades. The rating should not be read as doubt about the counts and rates themselves.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is right: the first-week peak is supported, and the authors themselves state the 91.0% figure and the release-day artefact in the main text. One correction to results_show: 'Across 18 cohorts, crude death rates were highest on days 2-7' should say that the time-period analyses excluded two cohorts (see missed).

missed: Which cohorts the time-period figures rest on. Figure 2's caption (p. 1785) says Cunningham and King (New Zealand's only cohort) and Binswanger (Washington) could not provide deaths by day and were excluded from the time-period analyses, and the text ties the days 2-7 rate 1612 and the more-than-1-year rate 737 to Figure 2 (p. 1783). So the days 2-7, weekly and later-period rates, and the cause-specific rates by period (657, 135, 71), rest on 16 cohorts in seven countries. The release-day rate (4036) must come from cohorts with day-level data. KF 4 and KF 5 and the interpretation gap's 'Across 18 cohorts' should say so; only KF 6's note mentions the exclusion.

How the 4-week split in KF 7 was defined. The paper does not say whether 'more than 4 weeks after release' (14,671 of 16,126) counts from the index release or from the most recent release, or whether the release day is included. A rough check (my inference, approximate because pooled rates are not crude totals): the pooled poisoning rates for days 2-7 (657), week 2 (about 400, Figure 2B) and weeks 3-4 (about 265) imply roughly 420 such deaths in the first 4 weeks after the index release among 1.47 million people, against the 1,455 implied by the paper. So the count probably uses time since each release.

can_establish ('deaths in custody recorded as release-day deaths inflate day-1 estimates') and outcomes.validity_norms ('Inspection of the data showed ...') state the miscoding as shown. The paper hedges it: the data 'suggested' some cohorts 'might have' miscoded (p. 1781), the day-1 spike is 'probably at least partially an artefact' (p. 1784), and such deaths 'may have been' miscoded (p. 1786). The comparison 4036 against 826 also sets different cohort sets side by side, and 826 has an interval of 0-3455. KF 8 words it correctly.

Addition to RI 5: the 'other and ill-defined' subcategories in Table 2 (1121 + 2818 = 3939) also fall 3 short of their category total (3942). The non-communicable and injury subcategories add up exactly.
